**Alberta's child poverty rate was 12.8% in 2024, the latest year available.** That is the share of people under 18 below the Market Basket Measure (MBM) poverty line, Canada's official poverty line.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, table 11-10-0135-01, "Percentage of persons in low income", Alberta, persons under 18, MBM (2023 base), vector v1792632015.
- **Trend (MBM, 2023 base):** 4.6% in 2020, 8.1% in 2021, 12.0% in 2022, 11.9% in 2023 and 12.8% in 2024. The very low 2020 figure reflects temporary pandemic income supports.

**Alternative measure:** the Low Income Measure after tax (LIM-AT) gives 13.9% for 2024. It was 13.5% in 2023 and 12.2% in 2022. Source: same table, vector v96520326.

I did not look up the Canada-wide rate, so I can't say how Alberta compares.

In Alberta's provincial and territorial public administration, average weekly earnings were **$1,883.03** in August 2026. That is the latest month available. It covers all employees and includes overtime, and the figure is not seasonally adjusted.

- **Annual equivalent:** about $97,900 a year, which is my own calculation (weekly figure × 52). Statistics Canada does not publish it.
- **Recent trend:** earnings were $1,694.36 in August 2025, so they are up about 11% over the year. They rose steadily from $1,667.49 in July 2025.
- **Scope:** the industry is NAICS 912, "Provincial and territorial public administration". It is government administration only. Teachers and health workers fall under other industries, so they are not included.

Source: Statistics Canada, Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, table 14-10-0203-01, vector v1560358 (Alberta, all employees, including overtime, NAICS 912). Reference period: August 2026.

I did not check hourly or salaried-only figures.

The average total income in Alberta was **$66,100** in 2024, the latest year available. This is for people aged 15 and over with income, and the figure is before tax.

- The median was lower, at **$48,100** for 2024.
- The average has barely changed since 2020: $66,600 in 2020, $67,500 in 2021, $66,000 in 2022 and $66,300 in 2023. These are not adjusted for inflation.

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0239-01, "Income of individuals by age group, gender and income source", Alberta, all ages and genders, total income, reference year 2024.
- Average income (excluding zeros): vector v107680657
- Median income (excluding zeros): vector v107680658

I haven't checked other measures, such as household or after-tax income, which would give different numbers.

Alberta's median total income was **$96,600** in 2024, the latest year in the table. That is before tax, for economic families and persons not in an economic family combined. After tax, the median was **$85,300**.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, table 11-10-0237-01. The vectors are v107654786 for total income and v107654846 for after-tax income.
- **Reference period:** 2024 (calendar year).
- **Trend:** The total-income median was $98,400 in 2023, $96,700 in 2022 and $100,200 in 2020, so it has been roughly flat for several years.
- **Not strictly "households":** The table's unit is the economic family or unattached person, which is close to but not identical to a household. Statistics Canada's own wording is "median income" of "economic families and persons not in an economic family".
- **Not checked:** I didn't pull the "economic families" only series, which would be higher than these figures.

In 2024, the latest year available, **12.8%** of Alberta children under 18 were living below the official poverty line (the Market Basket Measure).

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, table 11-10-0135-01, "Percentage of persons in low income", persons under 18, Alberta, Market Basket Measure (2023 base). Vector v1792632015.
- **Trend:** 4.6% in 2020, 8.1% in 2021, 12.0% in 2022, 11.9% in 2023 and 12.8% in 2024.
- **Different measure:** On the Low Income Measure after tax (vector v96520326), the 2024 rate is 13.9%. It was 7.5% in 2019 and 13.5% in 2023.

The 2020 and 2021 Market Basket Measure figures are unusually low. Pandemic-era income supports probably explain much of that, though I haven't checked this.

Alberta's provincial and territorial public administration paid an average of **$1,883.03 per week** in August 2026, the latest month available. This covers all employees and includes overtime. It works out to about $98,000 a year if you multiply by 52, but that is my own rough arithmetic, not a published figure.

- **Recent trend:** The weekly average was $1,667.49 in July 2025 and $1,877.58 in July 2026. That is a rise of about 12.6% over the year.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH), table 14-10-0203-01, vector v1560358. The series is "Average weekly earnings by industry, monthly, unadjusted for seasonality," for Alberta, all employees, including overtime, NAICS "Provincial and territorial public administration."
- **Scope:** The category includes territorial government administration, though that has little effect for Alberta. These are weekly earnings averaged across all employees, not hourly wages. I did not pull the hourly-paid-only series.

In 2024, the latest year available, the average total income in Alberta was **$66,100** per person with income. That covers people aged 15 and over, before tax, and excludes people with zero income.

- **Median:** $48,100 (vector v107680658).
- **Average over time:** $67,300 in 2019, $66,600 in 2020, $67,500 in 2021, $66,000 in 2022, $66,300 in 2023 and $66,100 in 2024. These are as published by Statistics Canada, and I haven't checked whether they are in current or constant dollars.
- **Source:** Statistics Canada, table 11-10-0239-01, "Income of individuals by age group, gender and income source", vector v107680657. Reference period: calendar year 2024. https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1110023901

The average is well above the median because a small number of high earners pull it up. This is individual income, not household income. If you want household income, tell me and I'll look up the household table.

Alberta's median total income was **$96,600** in 2024, the latest year available. That is before tax. After tax, the median was **$85,300**.

- **Source:** Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0190-01.
- **Vectors:** v96414571 for median total income and v96414651 for median after-tax income. These are the vector IDs the tool returned.
- **Reference period:** calendar year 2024.
- **Trend in median total income:** $100,200 in 2020, $97,600 in 2021, $96,700 in 2022 and $98,400 in 2023.

This table counts economic families and persons not in an economic family, not households. It is the closest match I found to household income, but the figure is not strictly a household median. I did not confirm whether the dollar values are in constant dollars, so check the table notes before comparing years.

Link: https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1110019001

In 2024, the latest year available, **12.8% of Alberta children under 18 were in poverty**. That uses the Market Basket Measure (MBM, 2023 base), Canada's official poverty line.

- **MBM, 2023 base:** 12.8% in 2024. The earlier values were 11.9% in 2023, 12.0% in 2022, 8.1% in 2021 and 4.6% in 2020. The source is Statistics Canada table 11-10-0135-01, vector v1792632015.
- **Low income measure, after tax (LIM-AT):** 13.9% in 2024. It was 13.5% in 2023. This measure is based on half of median income, so it is a different definition of low income. The source is the same table, vector v96520326.

The tool listed these series by month, but the data are annual and the reference period is the calendar year.

The MBM series, which uses the 2023 base, only has values from 2020. The rise from 4.6% in 2020 to 8.1% in 2021 to about 12% from 2022 on is partly due to the end of temporary pandemic benefits.

Table: https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1110013501
